authoredFrom: M60 reserved-word guard. Authored from a corpus measurement, 2026-10-02, not from reading the analyzer. `validation/m14/fixtures/bash/guard-ab-bash-calls.ts` over 200 hash-ordered corpus files found 30 of 2,945 emitted `calls` edges (1.02%) whose target is a POSIX reserved word — `if`, `then`, `elif`, `else`, `fi`, `esac`, `case`, `do` — every one of them produced by grammar recovery after the pinned grammar lost a construct, and none of them a command any script could run. The five source shapes here are verbatim corpus lines: kubernetes/cluster/gce/config-test.sh:468 (`if [[ -n ... ]]; then` with its `fi` in an unreadable fragment), kubernetes/third_party/gimme/gimme:935 (`if ! case "${GIMME_TYPE}" in`), ohmyzsh/lib/clipboard.zsh:66 (one line, `elif` and `then` together) and :945 (`esac; then`). The A/B also measured the ALTERNATIVE and rejected it: refusing every `calls` edge out of a damaged region removes 96 (3.26%) of which 15 are real calls to kube::log::status in kubernetes/test/e2e_node/gubernator.sh, so the guard is scoped to the NAME being a reserved word and nothing else. The positive expectation on /usr/bin/true is the half that pins that scope: it is a real command sitting in the same damaged region, and the over-refusing mutant bash/reserved-word-guard-over-refuses-builtins is caught by it.
